items.title: Want a New Elder Scrolls? Play Queen's Domain | IGN Quick Review
items.author: Michael Higham
items.content:
I'm a sucker for a good throwback to the early polygonal 32-bit era – Mouthwashing, Signalis, Crow Country, and Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun 2 are some recent favorites that come to mind. The latest one I've locked in on is Queen's Domain, a fantasy RPG that's as if an Elder Scrolls game was made for the PlayStation 1. Actually, it's explicitly inspired by FromSoftware's pre-Dark Souls series King's Field, where slow, deliberate first-person combat and exploration complemented punishing difficulty (which would later become FromSoft's signature, of course). But as much as Queen's Domain draws clear inspiration or shares similarities, it's a singular experience in 2026 that, so far, wields the intended friction of an old-school game wonderfully.

Washed ashore on a jungle island after your ship is sucked through the sea by a demonic queen, you're alone and in danger. Human-sized lady bugs and crickets lunge at you and follow you around, and the only thing you have to defend yourself in the early minutes is a rusted sword offered by a few survivors. Combat is tedious in these opening moments; avoid crickets by backpedaling when their animation starts, circle-strafe bugs when their wings flutter, and bunnyhop to hopefully avoid lasers shooting from those pesky eye plants stuck to the walls (which can shoot at you from a mile away). It's not an enticing or inviting start, but I had faith I'd strike a pile of gems if I just kept digging.

There are no quest markers, waypoints, or highlighted paths, just a rounded compass pulled straight out of King's Field. As someone who loves less handholding in exploration, I felt an obligation to see if Queen's Domain was doing this design philosophy justice. So, I pushed forward slowly, facing each enemy and navigating the tropical ruins carefully, waiting for a breakthrough as everything from resurrected skeletons to dragonflies wanted to kill me.

With just a faint glint on an off-shore mound, I found a belt of throwing knives to add to my measly arsenal. Important items are quite hard to identify in the world since they blend into the pixelated art style, so it took me longer than I'd like to admit to find these knives. Cool, I can finally kill those annoying eye plants, and also hit deep-seated switches next to big stone doors; one as a shortcut back to a save point and one to an underground crypt. You're not told to do any of this, but with enough poking and prodding at the world itself, you make these kinds of discoveries naturally.

Queen's Domain is a singular experience in 2026 that, so far, wields the intended friction of an old-school game wonderfully.

Along the way, I picked up a spear that does piercing damage and a wooden club to do blunt damage, both of which complement the slash damage of my rusted sword – which I'd also leveled up in proficiency just from using it. Now the weapon triangle came into focus: each enemy is weak, neutral, or resistant to different damage types, so weapon switching became part of the plodding combat dance. I should also mention that stamina is the biggest factor in damage output – each attack depletes the stamina bar, and the more stamina you have in store, the more damage you do. It recovers quickly, but you can't just spam attacks to get through enemies, which further emphasizes a calculated approach to combat.

In the underground crypt I mentioned, things started to flow smoother as I understood this dynamic and got better at reacting to attack patterns. Enemies designed to be primitive in the spirit of old games, with one-note attacks and predictable behaviors, and it's when you have to juggle multiple enemies where the more interesting challenge comes in. With the club's alternate attack, I could lunge at skeletons and get out of the way before they do their own lunging stab, and charging up my primary attack meant I could clear crickets in fewer swipes.

Since there are no autosaves and death means losing precious progress (save points are deliberately infrequent), finding a gate key at the end of the crypt raised the tension even further – now, I just needed to survive to make it back to my lone save point. This is another old-school design decision that, while it can be frustrating, complements Queen's Domain’s world design and the overall way it approaches challenge.

The key opened a gate back on a pier along the shore, which then led to a closed arena for the first real boss fight. I saw the screen-wide health bar pop up, and . The skeletal Shrine Guardian was bigger and more aggressive than anything before it, and caused knockdown with charged up sword slashes. Escaping its range was the toughest part and I got my ass beat the first try, but…aha! The spear's alternate attack is also a super-fast backdash, so what if I baited the boss and backdash-attacked, and then unloaded throwing knives while kiting it as I waited for my stamina to recover? Light work.

This highlighted the importance of alternate attacks, and defeating it rewarded me with a new, pristine holy sword with an alt attack that lets you briefly glide through the air. Sweet – higher damage, cooler looking, and a new way to explore… hold up, this opens up so many pathways I thought inaccessible! A broken bridge led to an important discovery for the main quest, as well as a new magic torch weapon; tree branches acting as platforms led to an area where I'd fight through waves of skeletons and bugs, and then use my magic torch to light up a tower needed to progress. Cryptic scriptures would poke at my curiosity about the world and lead me forward without outright telling me, and cracks in the sides of broken buildings contained actual rewards and key items like an airdash upgrade.

If I had to point to one thing I think is genius about Queen's Domain, it's the way its level design naturally guides you in exploration. In the absence of a map, you have to rely on examining the world for visual cues and remembering its layout. You'll need to commit to memory the areas you haven't fully explored and which paths you should return to after unlocking something new. What you're fundamentally asked to do isn't groundbreaking, but how it puts the onus on you to figure things out makes the experience so much more interesting.

Consumable healing items are scarce early on, and resting at save points respawns enemies – it's dangerous out there, and heading out to hopefully make progress is daunting. Issues like getting caught on geometry during attacks can be infuriating when survival is at stake, and some enemy types are just tedious to handle. A few frustrations can chip at my enthusiasm, but I'm willing to wade through those rougher waters because within these seemingly antiquated design principles is an RPG that's oddly refreshing and satisfying.

If I had to point to one thing I think is genius about Queen's Domain, it's the way its level design naturally guides you in exploration.

Moment-to-moment pacing changed quite a bit throughout the Water Temple area, which I cleared at about six hours into my playthrough. The dungeon crawling itself was paced really well; I never felt lost and the layout balanced being intuitive and provoking curiosity. It already dawned on me that this had a metroidvania edge with expanded abilities opening new paths forward; that much was clear when I got a second airdash upgrade here to cross a huge gap to make it to the last leg of the dungeon. I got a lot more comfortable with combat, feeling loosened up with a growing arsenal that included a dual damage-type morning star and the magic torch's fireballs. Even then, it contained some tough battles against poisonous sea creatures and pincer bugs throughout this lengthy dungeon, still requiring careful approaches informed by using your limited capabilities in smart ways – which would be further tested in the dungeon's boss fight against a corrupted king whale who spawned adds and crashed waves of poison water.

Emerging from the sewers afterward and lighting another tower, I found a teleporter that also indicated that I had at least eight more areas ahead. Now, I could firmly grasp the scope of Queen's Domain, and as I approached the next area, the cursed and spiraling library of the Tower of Knowledge, I felt this adventure was going to get deeper. But it's one where I was going to grow with it, evident in the way I took down its door boss, the Skeletal Executioner, with nary a scratch by dodging its axe projectiles, casting my torch, and charging my holy sword. I've entered a flow state.

Part of me is thinking about how it can keep up the momentum, handle power scaling, and evolve in ways that'll continue to surprise. From scavenging ancient coins for slicker weapons and charms to boost stats, those little rewards have been nice to chew on. Walking into a new region piques my curiosity as much as it instills an unsettling vibe, both intrigued and scared of what new enemies lie ahead. Each bit of progress showed me something new and built me up as a player in ways that weren't just leveling and a stat sheet.

What I thought was a straightforward homage to generations passed has so far been a smart twist on an old-school RPG experience. Queen's Domain is modernized in a way that doesn't compromise its adherence to being a tough, sometimes obtuse, throwback.

Queen's Domain is modernized in a way that doesn't compromise its adherence to being a tough, sometimes obtuse, throwback.

Audio design has been key in building atmosphere and complementing the pseudo-PS1 aesthetic, too. The crackling of fires are as detailed as the retro-sounding battle cries of enemies, footsteps having me checking corners and turning around just in case, and the not-so-fantasy but fittingly lo-fi soundtrack got some earworms I'm humming along to as I write this. This all may seem gimmicky on the surface, but there's intentional design that makes it stand out from so many retro-inspired games. (You can also smooth out the pixelated look if you want, but I'd argue it's necessary).

Yes, I know it's not an expansive open world with reactive NPCs, branching quests, and dialogue choices, but Queen's Domain is scratching that itch for first-person fantasy RPG combat that you'd get from Elder Scrolls. It's got some fantastic dungeon crawling and it’s also an interesting way to look back and better understand what King's Field was trying to do all those years ago through something palatable in the modern era. And these opening hours are illustrative of how smart level design and a good bit of friction can make for a unique experience that still has more beneath the surface.

It's been a hard-earned six hours, and there's so much more to see. If the bestiary is anything to go by, I've only encountered about 40 of the 188 enemies in Queen's Domain. This is going to be a long journey, but it's one I'm going to stay on until the wheels fall off. The thing I'm keeping in mind is if there's a deeper game underneath when the novelty wears off, and if it can sustain the sense of wonder it has delivered so far.

Of course, this is not a full review since this seems to be a massive game, but Queen’s Domain has the makings of a sleeper hit. If you're interested, it's available now for PC, PlayStation, Xbox, and Switch 2, and it's 20 bucks.

items.title: Yaga Episode 4 Recap and Review
items.author: Jessie Wade
items.content:
Warning: This review contains full spoilers for Season 1, Episode 4. Episodes 1-4 are now streaming on AMC+ in the US and Crave in Canada, with new episodes releasing on Fridays at midnight PT.

The latest episode of Yaga pulls out all the stops to create the most incredible entry in the series so far. It’s aptly named “Dance With The Devil.”

We begin with Rapp having another vision, this time of Pam mixing together a drug or potion in a lab while wearing a white coat and the sinister mask from Episode 3 over her face. As she opens her coat, we see she’s not wearing a top and has the Triskelion symbol tattooed on her sternum. Rapp blinks and immediately is brought back to the reality of sitting on the other side of an interrogation room at the police department, while Carson is pressing Pam about her involvement with Logan the night he died.

As Pam insists she did nothing wrong, she does admit to loving Logan, and that she had an intimate relationship with him even after he started obsessing over Henry, who she deemed as being “such a fucking narcissist” for loving the attention he received from Logan.

Clark Backo utterly glows as Carson in this episode – the balance of sweet and intimidating in her intensity while interrogating Pam is mind-blowing. We really get to see her step fully into her role and it’s phenomenal.

While Carson is pressuring Pam to cave and give any information she’s withholding, she tricks her into admitting to having a threesome with Henry and Logan. In shots of the intimate scenes, we hear from Pam how obsessed Henry is with himself, saying it was his idea and “he didn’t like the idea of someone taking something that belonged to him,” referencing Logan. We see Pam and Logan eventually having sex, while Henry watches and pleasures himself in the corner, with Pam saying that Henry said it was like “watching a movie of himself” and being utterly entranced by Logan.

A theme that’s developing more prominently in every episode is men in this show consistently becoming more creepy and perverted. We have Rapp hitting on basically everyone, Logan with his disturbing tape recordings last episode, and in this episode, Officer Eckert, played by Patrick Gilmore, makes several side comments alluding to his attraction to Pam, who is a noticeably younger woman compared to himself – not to mention a suspect in a murder case, which just shows how unhinged his attraction is.

In search of more concrete evidence, Rapp and Carson head to the motel to have a chat with Angel about her tattoo. She confirms it is a Triskele (a variation of the Triskelion) with multiple potential meanings: death, life, and rebirth; fertility; the triple goddess; and past, present, and future.

We learn about a new character, Laney – an older Ukrainian woman who makes pottery and holds sabbats (guided meditations) in the woods. She creates “Villy,” the drug powder Rapp had taken the other night, which keeps showing up in places, including in Henry and Logan’s house. Angel very clearly states Villy is a drug, but an “ethical organic dissociative tonic – a cure for every ailment” which we find out is made from chicken blood and human bone, and is taken during these sabbats for people to “manifest their dreams” and basically trip out.

Angel nonchalantly shares that, yes, Henry and Logan were both at these gatherings, piquing the interest of the buddy-cop duo, who fib to get more information out of her by any means necessary in order to find Laney.

As they drive to Laney’s house, the overhead drone shots where we see the car weaving through trees, and which are such a common motif in film and TV these days, take on a hauntingly beautiful feel which is enhanced by the entrancing score.

Carson and Rapp arrive at Laney’s house and, as they are peering around, they see someone fleeing from the premises. Unfortunately, they cannot identify who it is.

We see them searching carefully throughout Laney’s pottery studio and finding handmade jars that have the Triskele symbol on it – something Angel had said is “a mark of power.” Rapp comes across a worn-looking leather journal of Laney’s which is filled with sketches and recipes in Ukrainian – including what we now know to be the recipe for Villy. One of the sketches is of Baba Yaga’s house on chicken feet, and shockingly, another is of Henry wearing a flower crown while holding a chicken.

After digging for the whereabouts of Laney, they find out she’s at the hospital after suffering a fall, and are told she’s apparently delirious.

As Rapp and Carson arrive at the hospital, they find out Laney is, in fact, chaotically delirious, although it’s hard to tell how much of her character is deranged and how much she’s trying to deflect the questions Rapp is pressing her with, because she clearly knows things that are integral to finding Henry…

“He wants to dance with the devil.”

Rapp pushes her to share anything she knows about Henry, and as she sees a photo of him, she calls him a “bad dog” and says “he wants to dance with the devil.”

Carson steps into the hallway to answer a phone call from Eckert and finds out there was a video uploaded to Henry’s social media account. The utterly insane video shows Logan’s bedroom, complete with blood splattered around his window, as we saw last episode. The person recording shifts and moves the camera over the window ledge and we see Logan lying naked on the ground outside his bedroom window after he was allegedly murdered.

The person recording the video all of a sudden angles the camera onto a mirror in the room, seeing themselves in the reflection, wearing the creepy mask that appeared in Rapp’s visions more than once. They hold the shot on themselves for a few seconds before ending the video. Rapp and Carson now have a huge piece of evidence in Logan’s death that they need to decode.

We flip back to Rapp inside Laney’s hospital room, hearing him going back and forth asking her questions about Henry and “the devil” to get any type of answer. Laney keeps saying “wrong question!” over and over again like it’s a game. Then the music escalates, Laney’s heart rate spikes, the shots get tighter and faster going back and forth between them, and we finally hear Rapp yell “Who is the devil?!”... and everything stops.

Laney’s heart rate slows down as she grabs Rapp’s hand and kisses his palm saying, “Baba Yaga.” She cackles right before dropping back onto her bed as her heartrate flatlines. Laney’s dead.

items.title: Gentle Monster Review
items.author: Arnold T. Blumberg
items.content:
Gentle Monster is in limited theatrical release now and debuts on Netflix on Nov. 18.

A deeply unsettling drama, Marie Kreutzer’s Cannes premiere Gentle Monster follows a family living in the aftermath of disturbing allegations and the related moral compromises of the investigating officer. When her husband’s hard drives are seized on suspicion of child sexual abuse material (or child pornography), a French mother living near Munich tumbles down a rabbit hole of sharply penetrating uncertainties as the movie slowly folds in on itself, nudging you to question how you read its characters and their claims.

The film begins unassumingly, with musician Lucy Weiss (Léa Seydoux) comforting her German filmmaker husband Philip (Laurence Rupp) during his nervous breakdown; his burnout sees them moving to the suburbs sometime later. This introduction, along with tender scenes of Lucy and Philip raising their middle school-aged son Johnny (Malo Blanchet) in the lush countryside, endear us to this seemingly ordinary family and place us right in Lucy’s shoes as a woman with no reason to question her summery domestic bliss.

The inviting atmosphere is interrupted by an arriving German task force led by the stern, straightforward Elsa Kühn (Jella Haase), whose unit seizes Philip’s devices and asks him to follow them to their police station if he so chooses, with a lawyer by his side. Philip’s nervous reaction indicates he might know exactly why they have a warrant, but the shell-shocked Lucy is left to put the pieces of his charges together from information she gleans along the way, leading to startling scenes of silent reactions which make for powerful connective tissue. These moments, in turn, raise harrowing questions about how Lucy ought to approach her marriage and whether her son might’ve truly been safe all this time.

Excuses and explanations pile up, some more convincing than others, as the movie takes unexpected narrative detours before returning to its linear path involving Lucy’s dilemma. As she and Johnny move in with her mother (a kind but sharp-tongued Catherine Deneuve), she’s forced to keep the situation to herself as she tries to wade through the murky details. Meanwhile, as officer Elsa returns home to visit her own father (Sylvester Groth), his worsening mental state leads to instances of sexual impropriety with his live-in helper (Patrycja Ziółkowska), who has little recourse owing to the imbalance of power.

Although these two tales seldom intersect — except when Elsa looks into Phillip’s case or gives Lucy veiled advice — they’re bound thematically by the idea of women living in the blast radius of men’s actions. In Elsa’s case, the question of dementia either changing her father or revealing his latent impulses sends her into denial. This shutdown yields an apologism and compartmentalization similar to Lucy’s, who has to contend with the existential fear that she might not truly know someone she loves, and that she can’t simply flip a switch to stop loving him.

The women heading many of the film’s key departments — Kreutzer, cinematographer Judith Kaufmann, editor Ulrike Kofler, and composer Camille — create an atmosphere of comfort that slowly shatters. Their careful, tightly-controlled artistry avoids prescriptive social readings that might have been all too tempting when telling a story about gendered harm; instead, they capture the real and troubling waves of doubt and self-doubt — not to mention the grief-like negotiations — that can follow having to confront revelations this extreme. This leads the movie down a path of oblique, extended flashbacks that, rather than serving an informational purpose, simply allow us to observe the couple’s everyday dynamic as we, like Lucy, search these memories for hidden signs.

That the movie was shot on film serves an important thematic function to these scenes, in addition to creating an alluring, disarming texture. Philip shoots around the house on a 16mm camera as well, whose mechanical whir soundtracks some of these scenes, inducing a keen awareness of the camera’s presence. Kreutzer holds back on breaking the fourth wall with “her” camera except in thought-provoking moments; we’re led into the aforementioned flashbacks by literal flashes on the screen, the tangible light-leaks seen at the end or beginning of a celluloid strip, washing the image in hues of white and red. The more this happens, the more we’re led to question what we’re seeing (and our proximity to the characters) the same way we might question the footage shot by Philip, which Kreutzer continues to show us at important moments even after he’s accused.

Learning something new and horrifying about a loved one isn’t just about them. Feeling like you ought to have seen something can also dislodge your sense of self and judgement, which Seydoux approaches with remarkable naturalism, walking a heart-pounding tightrope between fearful rage and suffocating vulnerability. In addition to her performance in another Cannes competition entry this year, the unnerving body-swap thriller, the French actress has had a banner 2026 thanks to the commitment with which she lives and embodies each movie’s most difficult themes. She carries romantic love, maternal devotion, cautious fury, slow erosion of trust, and sheer spine-chilling terror all at once — in varying degrees and permutations — as Lucy is forced to fight her battle alone, searching for truths she hopes to find but which she may not wish to believe. That all this can be intuited from quiet close-ups alone makes Seydoux’s performance one of the year’s most fascinating and visceral.

It’s a bummer of a movie, but one whose most haunting moments may as well be philosophical thought experiments dramatized in cinematic form.  

Philip is a filmmaker who believes close-ups can eventually reveal hidden truths, while Lucy’s experimental pop deconstructions investigate male songwriters’ lyrics about love. Although neither one’s artistry is ever on full display in Gentle Monster — perhaps its only real disappointment — the mere verbal suggestion of these thematic aspects of their work primes the audience to scrutinize the characters in different ways, entering us into a conversation with Philip, Lucy, and the way they approach a world slipping out from under them like sand.

It’s a bummer of a movie, but one whose most haunting moments may as well be philosophical thought experiments dramatized in cinematic form. Granted, it occasionally gestures towards conclusions too neat and obvious, but the collective aftershock of its drama is undeniably affecting. Like the domino effect of Philip’s actions, it’s impossible to escape its lingering impact.

items.title: World of Warcraft: Forever Review So Far - Beta Impressions
items.author: Tom Marks
items.content:
This initial review-in-progress is based entirely on time spent in the pre-release beta, and will be updated as we get deeper into into the full game.

I was there, Gandalf. I was there when the World of Warcraft opened its servers for the first time in 2004 – which might not literally be 10,000 years ago, but sometimes it feels like it. And now that I've put a good 30 hours into the beta for World of Warcraft: Forever, I'm looking forward to today's launch in a way I haven't for almost any game in a long time. GTA 6 can wait.

It may surprise you to hear me say that and then follow it up with the fact that I had essentially zero interest in World of Warcraft: Classic back in 2019. In fact, I wrote one of my favorite articles ever about exactly why that was. But Forever is different. It's built on the bones of Classic, but with just the right amount of modern sensibilities baked in. There are new zones to discover, much-needed class changes, and some truly impressive graphical enhancements. So, I invite you to come on this journey with me, as it's going to be a bit different from our typical game reviews.

Blizzard really wants Forever to be about the journey, not the destination – and we plan to honor that in this review.

The thing is, Forever is made to be savored. I almost didn't want to review it at all, given how deadline pressure can sometimes warp the experience of something this big. Blizzard really wants this new take on their storied MMO to be about the journey, not the destination – and we plan to honor that here. This will be more of a long-form critique that's going to hearken back to an old Blizzard motto from their golden age: It will be done when it's done. Anything less wouldn't be a review of World of Warcraft: Forever so much as a review of rushing through World of Warcraft: Forever in a stressful and unintended way.

As such, I plan to update this piece as I climb my way to level 60 and discover all the new things there are to discover at the sort of pace I think would make sense if I didn't have a hard deadline. I still expect to have some kind of a firmer verdict before everyone wanders off for the December holidays. But if you want to know whether I think it's worth jumping in right now, on launch day, I can start by sharing my impressions from the beta.

As an avid player of Modern WoW until very recently, and someone who skipped Classic altogether, it's almost a revelation to open up my character sheet in Forever and see 23 years of what I can only describe as "streamlinesh**tification" stripped away. Like, dang, this used to be so much more of an RPG! All the modern game's stat pruning, summary execution of mechanics that added character but were demonized as "inconvenient," class role homogenization, and so much more added up to a death by thousands of cuts that you almost wouldn't notice if you stayed subscribed from the beginning because it was generally so gradual.I love having features like parry, block, and hit chance back. I love leveling up my different weapon skills when I hit a new level. I love that we have more secondary stats to worry about than just crit, haste, versatility, and mastery. I even love having to go buy my skill ranks every level, because it makes me learn where the hub for my class is in each major city and meet the key NPCs I can hang with and look up to. I love that levelling actually takes a long time. This was important stuff that was slashed to try and create a frictionless slope that would never alienate anyone ever, and the modern game is much poorer for having lost it.

Azeroth is so much more interesting to explore on foot, too. Flying mounts are fun, especially with the post-Dragonflight skyriding system. (They are!) But zooming around through the air as the default mode of travel has taken so much of the character of exploration and discovery out of Modern. Forever insisting that you spend the first 40 levels without even the speed boost of a ground mount allowed me to reconnect with this world in ways that really made me feel 14 again. It feels big and dangerous and mysterious. It's wonderful.

From what I've seen so far, I think they might have done it – let's see if they can keep it up to level 60.

And at this point, Forever's new lighting and post-processing make it look better than Modern to me. Yes, I do play with HD models. Sorry to all the SD purists, but I don't think the player races in particular actually hold up visually in 2026. I'm glad we can both pick the graphics we prefer. But regardless, these zones look stunning. They did go overboard with the fog in some areas, I think. But overall, I love the enhancements and going back to Modern feels like a straight downgrade.

I do have some concerns already. One of them is the "realmless" structure, which I think is particularly bad for roleplayers like me. We fought against capital cities having phasing in Modern for a good reason. Splitting up these hubs where people go to find RP tends to do the opposite of building strong communities. Blizzard has been swearing up and down that this is good for the long-term health of Forever. I am completely unconvinced so far, but willing to at least give it a chance.

It's hard to say too much more than that at this point. I ended my beta journey at level 13, gazing out across the dusty plains of Westfall, because I didn't want to spoil too much for myself before the big day. But from what I have seen so far? I think they might have done it. They made me believe I can go home again – and that home is somewhere I want to spend more time, with new surprises to discover. Let's see if they can keep it up for 47 more levels. Watch this space for updates in the weeks to come.

items.title: The Avengers #1 Review: A Marvel Relaunch Done Right
items.author: Jesse Schedeen
items.content:
Marvel's flagship Avengers series hasn't been in the greatest shape for the past decade. Even with very talented creators like Jason Aaron and Jed MacKay steering the ship, the franchise has struggled and largely failed to recapture the appeal of the Brian Michael Bendis and Jonathan Hickman eras. With this latest relaunch, Marvel has pinned all of its hopes on writer Chip Zdarsky and artist Marco Checchetto, the team responsible for one of the best Daredevil runs of the 21st Century. It turns out that they may be just the team to put this book back on track at long last.

Given the Daredevil pedigree, there was no way I wasn't going to be checking out this new series. That said, I did have certain reservations coming in. The team roster is oddly similar to that of Bendis' New Avengers run (albeit with the recently revealed Miracleman joining the fray). Is this merely a quick-and-dirty attempt at hearkening back to a better era for the series? Fortunately, there's a logic to which characters are included here, and the execution is different enough that this doesn't simply read like a retread of New Avengers, even if it definitely shares elements in common.

The basic idea here is that Zdarsky and Checchetto's Avengers chronicles the formation of a very different team in the wake of Avengers: Armageddon. The old guard have all tapped out for one reason or another, leaving the likes of Spider-Man, Wolverine, the aforementioned Miracleman, and a battered and brooding Captain Marvel to fill the void when the world cries out to be saved again. Like the 2004 New Avengers, this is a team brought together by circumstance rather than one that's been actively recruited. That generally seems to be the way to go for this franchise.

While there's only so much team-building that can be done in a first issue, Zdarsky wastes no time in taking advantage of these intriguing character dynamics. Obviously, we know he can write a mean Matt Murdock. But this isn't simply a retread of his past run. Zdarsky instead focuses on immediately forging a bond between Matt and Carol Danvers, the latter of whom is still adjusting to a new world where her powers are a shadow of their former self. I don't know if Daredevil/Captain Marvel shippers were a thing before now, but they certainly will be.

The creators also wisely hinge a lot of this first issue on Spider-Man. Spidey is very much the moral center of the book, the one most agitated by the absence of the Avengers and the generally frosty response the public has toward superheroes at the moment. Obviously, this isn't Spidey's first go-round as an Avenger, but this feels like a turning point for the character. His mantra about power and responsibility becomes all the more critical in a time when there's no one else to be an Avenger. Zdarsky understands these characters and what motivates them, and he makes the most of that in bringing the new team together.

And, yes, the book looks fantastic. Though that's hardly a surprise. Checchetto is coming off an incredible run working with Hickman on Ultimate Spider-Man, and he brings all the same strengths to bear on this new assignment. His figure work is stunning, as always, marked by elegant line-work, sunbtloy expressive faces and that trademark lovely hair only Checchetto can pull off. The general storytelling is equally impressive. Zdarksy's script gives Checchetto a nice balance of intimate character moments and large-scale action, and he handles both very adeptly. Matt Wilson's colors seal the deal, creating a tone that's both inviting and just a bit eerie where needed.

It's also worth pointing out how well this first issue integrates itself into current Marvel continuity. Not only does the series build very neatly out of Zdarsky's recent work on Armageddon and Captain America, but it reflects the current statuses quo of the various Avengers as the characters come together (including Spidey's current Aunt May predicament). Not in a way that punishes readers for not following the various other titles, but simply in a way that makes the current Marvel Universe feel a little more cohesive and united.

items.author: Arnold T. Blumberg
items.content:
receives a limited theatrical release on Nov. 6.

A gentle family drama told in the style of a sleazy New York indie, Jordan Firstman’s Club Kid is one of the year’s most self-assured gems. Picked up by A24 out of the Cannes Film Festival, Firstman’s directorial debut features him in the lead role of Peter Green, a washed-up gay Jewish club promoter who, at a personal and professional low point, discovers he has a ten-year-old son. The coming-of-(middle)-age story unfolds in and around New York’s bustling queer underground, which forms the colorful backdrop for a film of intimate emotional discovery, subdued heartache, and unexpectedly finding yourself through someone else’s eyes.

Opening ten years in the past with all the energy and misty allure of William Friedkin’s leather thriller, Cruising, the 35mm-shot Club Kid recreates the dim celluloid haze of ’70s and ’80s New York City with a more contemporary, upbeat lens. With one foot planted in queer culture’s past, Firstman depicts its liberated present through a hedonistic underground rave Peter organizes and attends, introducing us along the way to the movie’s catty ensemble. This includes his promoter business partner, Sophie (Cara Delevingne); his supportive ex-boyfriend, Devon (Nigil Whyte); and his ferocious trans DJ pal, Saffron (Saturn Risin9), among a cavalcade of other lively queens.

A drug-fueled threesome that evening, which Peter barely remembers, comes roaring back ten years down the line when an acquaintance from London drops off his surprise 10-year-old son, Arlo (Reggie Absolom). The kid’s mother has died, leaving him with no one else. Despite this morbid premise, Club Kid floats on a fabric of lurid, self-effacing comedy rooted entirely in character and community, starting with the gay Azerbaijanian teen and wannabe-philosopher, Nicky (Eldar Isgandarov), who Peter houses despite his own financial woes, and continuing through the aforementioned supporting characters introduced a decade prior, who all remain in Peter’s life.

The lengthy interim has seen Peter stall in arrested development, and his continued drug problems even lead to a professional falling out with Sophie right when Arlo shows up, leaving the new dad especially vulnerable financially and emotionally. A thirty-something with no direction, Peter is forced to reorient his life around fatherhood, a concept the polite 10-year-old Londoner seems remarkably more prepared for, though he disguises his grief beneath a dogged façade.

The more Arlo becomes a part of Peter’s life, the more the worlds of narcotics-fueled found family and unforeseen blood relation (and the responsibility it demands) collide for the fatigued impresario. In short, Peter needs to get his act together. But the party, and his desire to be at the center of it, has a certain magnetism he can’t ignore, to the point that the musically-talented Arlo soon begins showing up as an early-shift DJ alongside Saffron.

The film is absurdly funny and comes steeped in the postmodern, internet-meme-as-camp-culture queerness increasingly popular in online spaces and on TV shows like Drag Race while maintaining a consistent authenticity. Part of this is owed to the organic aesthetic approach of Firstman’s freewheeling handheld camera, which cinematographer Adam Newport-Berra nestles into tight spaces with incredibly fluid movements, making each scene of overlapping dialogue feel especially intimate. However, just as big a part of the film’s success is its naturalistic performance style. As Peter and Arlo, Firstman’s uncertainty and Absolom’s matter-of-fact-ness make for not only a knee-slapping comedy routine, but a mismatch of parental expectations through a subversion of vibe, energy, and traditional family dynamics, which Peter has to work especially hard to overcome.

It’s hard not to be sucked in by the familiar comforts of a movie as unique, good-natured, and downright charming as Club Kid. 

As the story goes on and the two get to know each other, the care they find in one another draws you in with its conversational quality. Long-hidden volatile emotions are gradually unlocked through Peter and Arlo’s chats and disagreements, as well as Arlo’s sessions with child therapist Oscar (the object of Peter’s interest, played by a smoldering Diego Calva). However, it isn’t long before the legal complications surrounding Arlo’s adoption across borders adds an additional rigorous layer to the saccharine drama. This gradually forces the salacious, sweetly taboo humor to subside in favor of a more piercing buildup of emotional tension, which mounts gradually until it eventually overflows.

Realism is often overrated in cinema. But when it harkens back to New Hollywood’s style while maintaining contemporary verisimilitude, it’s hard not to be sucked in by the familiar comforts of a movie as unique, good-natured, and downright charming as Club Kid, which wears its heart confidently on its bedazzled sleeve. In a mere two hours, it feels like an entire lifetime of love and heartache.

items.title: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Review
items.author: Tom Marks
items.content:
Two eras intertwine in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, and Nintendo skillfully commands them both. Link’s journey through the ages melds the world and dungeon design of classic Zeldas with the movement and presentation of its more recent games. This is not an exact one-to-one remake of the Nintendo 64 original, nor is it a complete reimagining. It’s a modern interpretation that adds depth to what was already there through its rich art style and expanded dialogue. Whether you're a returning fan approaching this as a remake of a longtime favorite or a newcomer viewing it with fresh eyes as a standalone adventure, Ocarina of Time is exceptional. I spent 30 hours obsessing over every inch of this beautiful realization of Hyrule – and when I reached the credits, I started over again to find even more of its best-kept secrets.

Link’s quest to stop the evil Ganondorf and save Hyrule proves how much value there still is in the traditional Zelda formula. That means exploring the world to find the next dungeon, unlocking a key item within that helps you solve puzzles and defeat its boss, and then using that tool to uncover new areas. There are also tons of secrets, side quests, and gold spiders to find off the main path. This more linear structure offers a different type of satisfaction than modern Zelda’s open-world adventures, and its signature time travel mechanic – which has you swap back and forth between child and adult versions of Link to progress, complete with a familiar but radically changed world for each – remains interesting to this day.

As soon as I stepped into Kokiri Forest, I was certain that this is the best Zelda has ever looked and sounded. From quaint towns to creepy dungeons to warmly-lit fields, this Hyrule has carved a permanent place in my mind. It’s rich with details that paint a full, practical picture of this fantasy world: Link takes a breath and moves his fingers when playing the ocarina, his scurrying Bombchu explosives are depicted as wind-up toys, and the grass he cuts blends naturally into the surroundings. It stays at a solid 60 fps practically the entire time, either docked or handheld, and it sounds fantastic, too. Gold Skulltulas fall out of trees with a loud thump, enemy swords sharply clang off Link’s shield, and Koji Kondo’s beautiful original soundtrack is perfectly performed by a talented small group of musicians.

Link’s animations are packed with endearing detail as well: he watches his step when running down stairs and covers his face when walking through tall grass. He also has some charming reactions pulled straight from Breath of the Wild: you can see him overheating in the volcanic Death Mountain Crater without the right gear, and his tunic will actually catch on fire. This is a small tweak from the original, where a timer warned you of how long he could survive the heat. Elements of modern Zelda’s reactive, systems-based design enrich this old-school adventure in small ways.

The way it’s presented has brought me even closer to this story than I was before – which is saying something for a game I play once per year. Important story moments are often beautifully framed, like how the opening seamlessly transitions from Link sleeping to his nightmare in Hyrule Field. Link remains a silent protagonist, but his adorable facial expressions tell me everything he’s thinking, like when he excitedly looks at his fairy sidekick Navi after being accepted by a new ally. Navi and the rest of the cast fill each scene with enjoyable, over-the-top voice acting that fits this fantasy world.

Snappy movement makes completing even the simplest tasks feel great.

The controls feel immediately familiar to Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom. While you can’t climb any wall – only ones clearly marked to allow it – Link can now freely dash and jump at the press of a button. You no longer have to line yourself up perfectly and perform a running auto jump, which transforms careful tightrope sequences into snappy platforming. He responds with precision, and the joy of moving through the world makes completing even the simplest tasks feel great.

Link wields his items from a third-person perspective, with optional motion aiming that turned me into a sniper. Freely aiming and moving at the same time makes weapons like the slingshot or bow far more viable parts of your arsenal. I’ve probably fired more slingshot pellets across my two playthroughs of the remake than in every run of the original combined. There was one moment where I was thinking about how much I liked using the slingshot now that I completely forgot to jump – thinking Link would do it on his own – and nearly fell off a high bridge. (Thank goodness Link bailed me out by clinging onto the ledge.)

Your main weapon is still your sword, and combat feels great; Link is quick on his feet, and his slashes land with crunchy, bright impact. You need to learn each enemy’s behaviors and swiftly sidestep or backflip away until it’s the right time to strike back. Wolfos swing their claws so hard they twirl around, while Stalfos grant a window of opportunity while they’re recovering from a jump attack. Each enemy is a light puzzle of its own.

This pattern recognition could get old – once you’ve seen one Dodongo do a spin attack, you know how to beat them all – but Hyrule has a wide lineup of colorful enemies that only appear in a few places each. Baby Dodongos chase you and explode like fireworks, Armos statues come to life and jump scare me every time, while fully armored Moblins charge at you with sharp spears. Well… they’re fully armored in the front. In the back, all you can really see is a thong. It hits the amiibo collecting part of my brain to beat each enemy type and install its statue at the new Hall of Fallen Foes, a museum that lets you admire the detailed character designs and rematch powerful enemies.

I’ve never viewed the Zelda series as combat games first: they are action-adventure games with equal parts combat, exploration, and puzzle solving, so the relative simplicity of the action here works well. That said, this remake isn’t very challenging, and part of that actually ties into how well it controls. The small number of enemies in each fight and the way they act are still largely grounded in 1998 game design that was perfectly tuned for teaching people how to move and fight in an early 3D space. Now, Link feels better to control than he ever has, but the enemies haven’t risen to meet him. I always enjoyed the fights – especially tense two-on-one encounters in claustrophobic spaces – but I rarely felt at risk of failing. This applies to minigames and side objectives as well: it was routine for me to get the top prize at the shooting range, race track, or bowling alley on my first attempt when motion aiming, free camera control, and better movement were all on my side.

It feels like a missed opportunity to not have the harder Hero Mode that Skyward Sword HD, Echoes of Wisdom, and the Link’s Awakening remake all had at launch. Aside from upping the difficulty, it would also give value to a new item the remake introduces. Business Scrub Seeds let you summon a shopkeeper at a moment’s notice to restock on health or items. Their description reads that they “emit the overpowering scent of business,” which is a great line. But resources are so plentiful that I never had to use one, and opening a secret treasure chest only to find one of these seeds always led to a brief feeling of disappointment. That would probably change in a Hero Mode where hearts came at a premium. Instead, Ocarina of Time’s one-size-fits-all approach to difficulty left me wanting a bit more.

Link’s capabilities are modern, but the world he lives in is delightfully old-school.

Link’s capabilities feel modern, but the world he lives in is delightfully old-school. On my way to the dungeon where you unlock bombs, I must have passed 10 cracked walls begging to be blown up. Once I cleared the dungeon and had 20 bombs in my pocket, it was rewarding to return to each one and reveal its secrets.

This style works especially well in Ocarina of Time because of Hyrule’s dense, compact layout. It never feels like a chore to return somewhere once you have new abilities because everything is so close together. Once you figure out how to ride your horse, Epona, Hyrule Field becomes a playground that’s fun to zip across. Plus, you may stumble into smart shortcuts that tie distant areas together, and you’ll learn songs that let you warp to specific spots.

My curiosity guided the adventure: Navi rarely interrupts the action with unsolicited advice, and the newly-added quest log only gives broad descriptions of your next objective, like “Find out what’s going on in Zora Domain.” So while you may not be able to get endlessly sidetracked with self-driven quests like in newer Zeldas, it’s great that it still falls on you to discover the path forward. Exploration has always been at the heart of this series – it just takes different forms.

You often find out what’s going on the old-fashioned way: talking to people. Hyrule is full of secrets, and its townsfolk love to gossip. A helpful Zora heard the king is worried about his daughter, which leads me to the next dungeon. A woman in Kakariko Village is looking for her lost Cuccos, and reuniting them nets me a nice prize. A Goron admits he licked his tribe’s sacred ruby, and that it was saltier than he thought it’d be. Conversations led to main quests, side quests, and funny moments I won’t forget.

Characters say new things based on the latest story beat, and they even have more fleshed out daily routines since time now passes when you’re in towns. They basically just walk between where they stand during the day and where they are at night, but I guess the gossipy culture got to me, too, and I obsessed over knowing everybody’s business. I watched from the rooftops as time passed by below.

These characters send you toward side activities where you play games, investigate things that look out of place, and draw connections across the world and its eras. Their wonderful variety plays into the excellent pace, where it always felt like I was doing something different. But no matter where I was, I kept an eye (and ear) out for well-hidden Gold Skulltulas. Side quests help fatten your wallet, and you'll need as much cash as you can get, because Great Fairies charge a pretty hefty price for worthwhile magic upgrades.

Traditional Zelda dungeons are still a delight to unravel.

Eventually, all that adventuring will lead you to a dungeon. I’ve really missed traditional 3D Zelda dungeons, which often feel like puzzle boxes that are designed to be solved in a specific way. There is beauty in the freedom of modern Nintendo design, where any answer that works is a correct one. But there is also beauty in limitation, where figuring out the only solution can be just as rewarding as inventing one yourself.

When Zelda series producer Eiji Aonuma was in college, he made mechanical wooden dolls that could dance and play musical instruments – he said he loved when people would see them and wonder what kind of tricks were inside, and how all of their parts functioned together. One of Aonuma’s first projects at Nintendo was to lay out Ocarina of Time’s original dungeons, and I can easily see the parallels between his two types of creations. The best dungeons act as one big contraption, forcing you to think of the room you’re in as part of a larger whole, where decisions and discoveries in one area impact another.

28 years later, these dungeons are still a delight to unravel. They carry an excellent blend of puzzles within individual rooms, battles with enemies and minibosses, and clever moments where you need to zoom out and think about the whole space. Each one feels unique: Navigating twisted hallways in the Forest Temple leads to different wings of a haunted mansion, while the Fire Temple’s eerie chants wonderfully complement its intense linear climb to the top of a scorching tower.

I never get tired of entering a new room, taking out the enemies within, and then figuring out what it’s asking of me, like which block I need to push where or what switch I need to hit next. However, there are a number of small changes that add up to make a big difference in how these dungeons feel to work through, not always for the better. For example, a few locks are now placed on doors closer to their respective keys. This effectively shrinks the explorable space in these moments – if you run into a locked door and don’t have the key, there aren’t that many rooms it could realistically be in. It doesn’t ask you to think about the broader layout quite as much as a result.

I understand taking the opportunity to tone down pain points that people have been getting stuck on for nearly 30 years. But this remake tends to overcorrect: a few rooms that used to have admittedly obscure solutions now contain really obvious ones. In some cases, literal guard rails make sure you don’t miss the only possible answer in front of you. Puzzles that require a specific item are oftentimes overly telegraphed. For example, even though the hookshot will latch onto lots of surfaces, several places where you used to have to figure out you needed it have been replaced with the unmistakable hookshot target. This removes some of the required thought: you recognize the symbol, and equip the proper item. This has always been part of Zelda, but it’s exaggerated here.

The Water Temple – which is easily the original’s most infamous dungeon – has fewer small keys altogether. An easy-to-miss room that used to hold a key is now only required for completionists, which takes a huge moment of discovery off of the critical path. It’s not like every room has been changed in this way, but there are enough instances that they amount to a noticeable trend, which makes the big Zelda “aha!” moments when you overcome something less frequent and less special.

Many pain points have been toned down, but this remake tends to overcorrect.

This is why I played the entire game twice before writing this review. I wanted to see how the dungeons felt when I wasn’t so closely scrutinizing their differences. Even with fewer keys, the Water Temple does still successfully test your logic skills as you shift the water level to manipulate its accessible areas. Some individual puzzles have even been improved over their original forms. So I don’t want to cause panic: the dungeons are still largely fantastic. I just wish they trusted me more.

I also played on Pro Mode the second time around, which removes almost all UI elements, including the minimap. It’s easy to watch the really detailed minimap like a GPS to see exactly where the chests and locked doors are in the current room. If you’re a Zelda expert, I recommend turning it off from the start – you can still pause and see the map if you need to.

The dungeon bosses are giant, threatening puzzles to be solved, usually with a specific item. They go down fairly quickly once you know their tricks, but I don’t mind when part of the fun is racing to improve my time in the boss rush mode. These fights are filled with epic moments, like knocking an enormous spider off the ceiling. Or, you can find goofy ways to fight them instead, like deflecting Phantom Ganon’s volleys with an empty bottle instead of a sword, a wonderful detail I’m so happy to see return.

That is just one of dozens of little surprises that make Ocarina of Time so special. Hyrule is filled with secrets that exist Certain ocarina songs trigger interactions that have no purpose other than playfulness. Link can wear masks that change what people say, sometimes revealing shockingly dark secrets. You dive into underground caves to find hidden treasure, but sometimes there’s just a cow down there! You’ll hear rumors of alternative ways to kill enemies you’ll wonder how you ever lived without. There are conversations you can only hear at very specific points that feel really special when you manage to catch them. Ocarina of Time does not care if you miss some of its secrets, which makes stumbling into them all the more impactful. I’m sure it’s hiding some things that are still a secret to everybody.

items.title: Marvel's VisionQuest Episode 7 Review: 'Immolation'
items.author: Jesse Schedeen
items.content:
Paul Bettany may nominally be the star of VisionQuest, but we can all probably agree that this has largely been The James Spader Show up until now. Spader's gleefully acerbic Ultron has been the best and most pressing reason to follow the series. But we shouldn't count out Bettany. He has a lot to bring to the table, and Episode 7 allows him to really stretch his legs and prove that he can dominate the screen every bit as capably as Spader.

"Immolation" opens with a WWII-era flashback, where we finally meet the elusive Phineas Horton in the flesh. And - surprise, surprise - he turns out to be played by Mr. Bettany. This is the first of several opportunities Bettany has to play a different character in Episode 7, and he doesn't waste it. There's such a palpable sense of haunted suffering emanating from Horton in this scene, and it nicely sets the tone for the rest of the episode.

From there, the show forces Vision to look inward and finally deal with all the emotions and memories he's been suppressing since he first climbed off that operating table at S.W.O.R.D. If VisionQuest is literally about the character undertaking a stereotypical vision quest, then this marks the point where he consumes a bunch of peyote and goes off in search of true enlightenment.

I enjoyed the way Vision's descent into his own mind is framed here. It feels a bit like the MCU doing a riff on Hideo Kojima's P.T. Vision keeps circling the same hallways, with each loop bringing an extra dose of dread and psychological unease. I've mentioned this before, but it's really fun how the series chooses to give visual representation to the complex digital processes unfolding in the minds of Vision, Ultron, and Jocasta.

During this journey inward, Bettany gets the chance to switch roles again and play the classic, pre-Infinity War Vision. That makes for a very entertaining clash between Visions. I won't say Bettany's two performances are wildly different here, but there is a subtle distinction to how he plays the older, wiser, more emotionally well-adjusted Vision.

There is a subtle distinction to how Bettany plays the older, wiser, more emotionally well-adjusted Vision.

All of this psychological turmoil culminates with White Vision getting to the root of his subconscious and encountering not just the digitized remains of Horton, but also his signature creation, J.I.M. All these years removed from Captain America: The First Avenger, it's quite a treat to see the original Human Torch (not that he's named as such here) introduced as an actual character and not just a background prop.

It's here that Bettany really digs in and starts chewing some scenery. You have to admire his ability to take what is essentially four variations of the same character and make each into such distinct roles with their own vibe and cadence. And even just in terms of White Vision, it's a nice change seeing him dig into the emotion of the role and let loose everything the character has so carefully bottled up over the years. This episode is truly Bettany's finest hour on the series so far.

Comparatively, the rest of Episode 7 is a bit underwhelming. On the Ultron/Jocasta front, we just don't spend enough time with the characters for their parallel journey to resonate as strongly as Vision's does. That all ends too abruptly for its own good. As for the events unfolding in Paladin's (Todd Stashwick) hideout, it gets the job done as far as adding a bit of extra drama and tension to Vision's jorney, but it's very much secondary to the real meat of "Immolation."

Things certainly end on an inriguing note, though. We finally meet Paladin's elusive benefactor, and he's not Phineas Horton or J.I.M., as expected. Who is this seemingly human version of Ultron? We'll surely find out in the finale next week.

items.title: The Remarried Empress Episodes 1-4 Review
items.author: Arnold T. Blumberg
items.content:
This is a spoiler-light review of the first four episodes of The Remarried Empress, which are now available to stream on Disney+.

In the streaming wars, Disney has the obvious and not insignificant edge on princess stories. However, that edge tends to come in their kids/family content, which makes their biggest Korean drama swing yet — a big-budget romantasy epic called The Remarried Empress — kind of a brilliant programming decision. The 10-episode series is a live-action adaptation of a very popular web novel-turned-webtoon; the latter has accumulated almost three billion views on Naver. While technically the main character is an Empress and not a Princess, try telling that to her dresses, her gaggle of ladies-in-waiting, and her Beauty and the Beast-esque ballroom dance scene.

The Remarried Empress stars Hometown Cha-Cha-Cha's Shin Min-a as Navier, the elegant empress of the fictional Eastern Empire and wife to Emperor Sovieshu (The Trauma Code’s Ju Ji-hoon). Navier and Sovieshu share a respectful if not particularly passionate marriage, maintaining a stable royal leadership for the Eastern Empire. However, they have yet to have a child. When Sovieshu rescues escaped slave Rashta (The Red Sleeve’s Lee Se-young) from bounty hunters, he quickly falls for her, forcing Naiver to accept Rashta as an imperial mistress.

In a more stereotypical princess story, rags-to-riches Rashta would be the aspirational protagonist, and there’s a lot of potential in subverting that trope. However, The Remarried Empress does not live up to it, in large part due to the shallowness of its characters. The K-drama tries to give Navier more emotional interiority than her webtoon counterpart, but seems ultimately unwilling to stray too far from the source material characterization to make Navier particularly sympathetic in the first four episodes.

The result is a lead that is not particularly fun to root for. Though Navier may be beautiful and played by the likable Shin, it’s hard for a peasant like myself to care that the empress’ pride has been slighted and her commitment to the noble hierarchy upset. Perhaps another genre or a more masterful script could convince me to judge Emperor Sovieshu for his choice to chase love rather than duty, but The Remarried Empress is a romance, which means it needs viewers to believe that love is one of the most powerful forces of all and should be valued above most else. As the episodes progress, Sovieshu and Rashta become more and more like cartoon villains, securing a likability-by-comparison for Navier that is effective in building some sympathy.

Another potential path to establishing more gripping stakes would necessitate articulating the political stakes of disruption in the imperial marriage, or why Navier cares about having political power. However, at least in the first four episodes, it’s unclear what the Eastern Empire — or Navier — stands to suffer politically from the imperial divorce teased in the show’s title. The Remarried Empress premiere offers a peek at the fantastical danger in the kingdom when a massive worm-beast almost kills Navier while she and Sovieshu are out for a hunt. She is saved through her own skill and the help of enigmatic and handsome Prince Heinrey (Romance is a Bonus Book’s Lee Jong-suk), when he is in his secondary form as a bird; yes, a bird. These glimpses at magical world-building are intriguing, but don’t pay off in any cohesive way in the first act of the season.

The momentum suggested in the first episode does build when Prince Heinrey properly enters the narrative in his human form. In the first few episodes, he fosters a relationship with Navier solely as a bird, delivering messages to the empress from a mysterious admirer (i.e. him). In these encounters, the notorious ladies’ man begins to fall for the beautiful and lonely Navier. While Navier begins to see the bird as a confidante, she does not yet know that the creature she cares for and shares her secrets with is actually a human man, let alone the next in line for the throne of the Western Kingdom.

When Heinrey-as-human finally arrives at the Eastern Empire court, along with nobility from other empires for a New Year’s Celebration, The Remarried Empress utilizes some killer historical-romance-on-screen shorthands to great effect. When Navier and Heinrey share a dance in a ballroom of their royal social circle, it builds on the cinematic language crafted by Pride and Prejudice adaptations and recently utilized by Bridgerton to instantly communicate authentic, romantic intimacy. More broadly, the charismatic irreverence of Prince Heinrey’s character brings a much-needed levity to the self-serious triangle of Navier, Sovieshu, and Rashta, and his instant devotion to Navier gives us something more substantial to root for.

The interplay between these four main characters is helped immensely by the quality of this cast and by the lavish production design and setting. The Remarried Empress seemingly spared no expense in bringing the fantasy romance to the screen. Unlike most Korean historical fantasy dramas, Remarried Empress' palace setting is inspired by European architecture, fashion, and etiquette, and was filmed in the Czech Republic and Germany to capture a Western aesthetic. This blend of a Western-inspired fantasy setting with a Korean cast and story sensibility gives The Remarried Empress a unique watchability, even if it doesn’t have anything particularly interesting to say about power or politics thus far.

In a global streaming landscape that takes so few big swings on romantasy series, we can’t be too hasty about dismissing a series like The Remarried Empress.

The Remarried Empress also benefits greatly from the current dearth of big-budget romantasy series. Despite the massive success of book series like A Court of Thorns and Roses, we have gotten so few big-budget TV shows in the genre, which speaks to Hollywood’s broader devaluing of romance-centric storytelling over the past few decades and women as our own audience. While this is beginning to change in no small part due to the massive, proven success of Korean dramas around the world, we have yet to see a breakout hit. Netflix’s Shadow and Bone had immense potential, but was canceled (despite its strong viewership) before getting to the main Six of Crows storyline, widely considered to be the meatiest part of Leigh Bardugo’s Grishaverse; I still lament.

So far, The Remarried Empress is nowhere near as good as Six of Crows, though it might be on par with Shadow and Bone; I hope it gets a chance to evolve in a way the Shadow and Bone adaptation never did. In a global streaming landscape that takes so few big swings on romantasy series, we can’t be too hasty about dismissing a series like The Remarried Empress. In its first four episodes, it has yet to live up to the potential of the immense creative and financial resources invested in it, but what’s a princess story for if not believing in a happier ending?

items.title: The Cat in the Hat (2026) Review
items.author: Arnold T. Blumberg
items.content:
Having received a 2003 live-action adaptation that , the Cat in the Hat is back with a new feature film. This time, it’s in animated form, and fortunately the end result is a much better one.

With Mike Myers having starred in the live-action version, another group of filmmakers have once more turned to a Saturday Night Live alum, with Bill Hader now voicing the Cat. Dr. Seuss's beloved children's book is far too short to make for a feature-length story on its own, so things are rather drastically reinterpreted and expanded upon here, with writer-directors Erica Rivinoja (South Park, Borat Subsequent Moviefilm) and Alessandro Carloni (Kung Fu Panda 3) essentially just taking the basic idea of the fantastical Cat in the Hat appearing to children to encourage imagination and mischief.

The opening scenes feel somewhat similar to Monsters, Inc., establishing an entire imagination-based business of sorts with the Cat in the Hat as an employee. Other anthropomorphic animals work alongside him, all in the service of providing entertainment and encouragement to kids needing an imagination boost. Fortunately, the film doesn’t get too bogged down in the “company” scenario, mostly using it as a fun way to incorporate nods to the Seuss-y source material in the form of rhyming rules explained by staff members (voiced by the likes of Giancarlo Esposito, Bowen Yang, and Quinta Brunson), along with some visual depictions of the Cat in that Hat that also harken back to the book. From there, the story follows the Cat appearing to sister and brother Gabby (Xochitl Gomez) and Sebastian (Tiago Martinez), who are trying to deal with moving to a new city with their mother, Carmen (America Ferrera).

The Cat in the Hat shows genuine creativity from the start, beginning with its distinct visual interpretation of its two worlds. The realm the Cat and his colleagues live in appears much more bright, colorful, and off-kilter compared to the more realistic and muted feel given to Gabby and Sebastian’s apartment life. The film thankfully provides solid laughs on a fairly frequent basis too, from sight gags and slapstick that can entertain all ages to some notably multilayered jokes that can easily work for kids but arguably hit harder for the adults in the audience.

It also certainly helps to have Bill Hader voicing the Cat, bringing his deft sense of humor to the role along with his ability to do impressive voices. In addition to Hader, the movie has a bit of a cheat code in the form of Matt Berry (What We Do in the Shadows) as the voice of Gabby and Sebastian's pet fish, Waffles, who the Cat promptly gives the ability to speak. Is there a greater and more innately funny voice than Berry's these days? Hearing his bombastic delivery as an overwhelmed and frustrated fish is continually funny.

The film’s storyline involves the Cat introducing and then promptly losing a device that functions in a manner similar to Doctor Strange's Time Stone, enabling the user to rewind recent events. The search for this device takes the Cat, Gabby, and Sebastian inside incredible versions of the moving boxes that still fill the kids’ apartment; they travel through worlds where everything inside these boxes appears larger than life, often having actually come to life in the form of various toys, objects, and drawings they encounter. While some of this is a bit reminiscent of the journey through the mind in Inside Out, there are a lot of unique and appreciated touches throughout as everything from musical instruments to IKEA instructions can and do express themselves in various ways.

Despite overstaying its welcome, The Cat in the Hat remains easy to enjoy thanks to its likability and humor.

The one big drawback with the film is that it’s simply too long for its subject matter, losing energy as it nears its conclusion. Running just a few minutes shy of two hours, it starts to drag in its third act; an obvious reason for this is that there are just too many overlapping conflicts introduced. The film is ultimately juggling the Cat’s quest to get back his lost device; a monstrous creature called “Something” who is pursuing our heroes; the fact that the Cat in the Hat's job is in jeopardy thanks to recent screw-ups; and another subplot about Carmen’s snooping landlord (Paula Pell), who is itching for a reason to evict the new family in the building thanks to her strict rules. It feels like Rivinoja and Carloni overcompensated for how slight the book is; the movie would have been better served by dropping at least one of these storylines, as the movie feels noticeably stretched out as it nears its resolution.

Still, despite overstaying its welcome, The Cat in the Hat remains easy to enjoy thanks to its likability and humor. That includes how it makes use of the book’s popular Thing 1 and Thing 2 characters, who are expanded here into a large group of similar Thing creatures that the Cat unleashes into Gabby and Sebastian’s apartment. These weird little guys have an amusing and wacky Gremlins-type chaotic energy, even as you can feel the studio salivating at the chance to turn the Things into the next Minions. But being aware of that is made easier when you’re watching an often sly film like The Cat in the Hat, which provides its own very good meta joke that acknowledges this fact with a wink.

items.title: Wild Horse Nine Review
items.author: Scott Collura
items.content:
Two killers head out on a not quite break-from-work trip to a picturesque location, where shenanigans ensue. I've seen that movie and it's called In Bruges, you might be saying. But In Bruges writer-director Martin McDonagh is far from playing the same Funny Games as Michael Haneke by making the same film twice, so while his new film Wild Horse Nine might put him in familiar territory, this is not just another In Bruges -- and we are all the better for it.

The Catholic guilt remains, but McDonagh trades the tortured hitmen of In Bruges for two CIA spooks who need a reprieve from setting up Augusto Pinochet's coup in early '70s Chile. So off they go for a quick breather from working to overthrow a democratically elected Marxist (the CIA can't have that, no. Definitely not in their own hemisphere!) to see the big heads on Easter Island.

What makes this film great is its ability to tackle heady subjects like political violence and CIA-backed regime change and yet still be funny as hell and a great hangout movie. It's a tough needle to thread, but Martin McDonagh does it without being insensitive to the real-world changes that are happening around his characters.

Petty. Brilliant. Bickering.

McDonagh is an excellent filmmaker, but he’s undoubtedly best at screenwriting. His dialogue is incredible. It can be absurd, funny, charming, mean, and insightful; most of the time, it can be all of those at once. I've been using some form of "You're a nice guy, Pádraic" as my preferred euphemism for calling people an idiot ever since I saw The Banshees of Inisherin. It's such a nice, pleasant veneer, but it's so cutting. And when I use it, most people don't realize I'm insulting them, just like Pádraic.

Wild Horse Nine is also chock-full of great zingers. Take the scene in the trailer, where Lee (Sam Rockwell) is trying to shush Chris (John Malkovich), who won't stop talking about all his political assassinations.

Chris snaps back, "I've killed people in countries you can't even spell," and then mentions that he killed a guy in Czechoslovakia.

"You never killed anyone in Czechosl-fucking-vakia. You just know I can't spell it," responds Lee.

Those micro-tugs-of-war for power, jockeying for a kind of dominance that's ultimately inconsequential, are a hallmark of McDonagh's writing and what make his dialogue so memorable. It's part lyrical, part petty, and even takes on elements of stand-up comedy like the callback.

For example, some of the film's best jokes are set up early with pithy lines, only to be paid off later. And in a true test of a film's quality, McDonagh didn't burn off the best moments of dialogue in the trailer.

Of course, McDonagh's dialogue is only half the equation. A script is only as good as the hands of the performers it's in, and McDonagh has assembled a great cast.

Sam Rockwell is back, collaborating with the director who helped him win his Oscar for 2018's Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri. This time he's playing Lee, a spy whose loyalty is torn between his partner and his agency.

John Malkovich co-stars as Lee's partner and the more seasoned spy, Chris. The CIA was doing tons of meddling in the '60s and '70s, and Chris was boots on the ground for a lot of it. All that experience combined with his wildcard nature is what's pushing Steve Buscemi's MJ (the head of the CIA's South American operations) to believe he's a real liability and insist, "He ain't leaving the fuckin' island." (Can you blame the guy? He's talking about killing people... on an airplane.)

Listening to these two bicker is the absolute best part of the film.

Lee and Chris's relationship is a cockeyed mix of Obi-Wan and Anakin and part Riggs and Murtaugh. Malkovich's Chris is both the old, grizzled Murtaugh and the maverick Riggs combined into one CIA spy. Meanwhile, Lee is the well-meaning Padawan who is on the verge of having to make some hard decisions.

Whether Chris is pontificating on why "gay countries make the best cheese" or clowning on Lee for all his wife's infidelities, Malkovich has most of the film's best lines. (Speaking of which, Parker Posey is absolutely hilarious as Lee's wife Margie.) Listening to these two bicker is the absolute best part of the film. That's all thanks to Malkovich and Rockwell's chemistry, which makes these scenes feel like the effortless banter of old colleagues.

Quips aside, Malkovich deftly handles a complex, multifaceted character with empathy and charm. Without getting into too much detail, Chris knows he isn't long for this world, and, like the flawed Catholic he is, he's seeking a bit of redemption on his way out. He's said some bad things, done some worse things; his ability to piss off literally every character in the film is unrivaled. But Malkovich's charisma keeps us invested in him, and by the end, we're rooting for him.

The film's redemptive tension is best exemplified by Chris's relationship with Monica, one of the young progressive women he insults at the airport. Played by Chilean actress Mariana di Girolamo, Monica is essentially the heart of the film. Despite being completely repulsed by Chris's antics, they keep running into each other on the island, and eventually it's Monica who really forces Chris to confront his past and draw out what's left of his humanity.

I can't help but compare this film to In Bruges. In many superficial ways, they're extremely similar, but the comparison also helps emphasize how much Martin McDonagh has improved as a storyteller. It's not like he was bad before; In Bruges, with its funny but generic hitmen on the lam, was one of the better aughts crime flicks that were trying to duplicate Pulp Fiction's success over a decade later.

Wild Horse Nine and In Bruges share themes of guilt, redemption, moral codes, and loyalty. But where In Bruges confines its moral reckoning to the personal, grounding Wild Horse Nine in historical events adds an extra layer of thematic depth. Using the lead-up to Pinochet's coup as the backdrop for Lee and Chris's misadventures on Easter Island forces the characters to confront the moral culpability of their actions, while also challenging American audiences to reckon with the enduring consequences of their country's political meddling.

To put a finer point on it, it's extremely tough for a film to have me laughing at two CIA agents debate who would be a bigger security risk to the agency, a boozer wife or a heroin wife, and also get me to wiki Patrice Lumumba immediately after walking out of the theater. But that's what makes Wild Horse Nine stand out: it makes the absurdity of these men entertaining without letting you forget the very real consequences of their work.

Cinematography That Evokes a '70s Aesthetic

If you're like me, you go see a Martin McDonagh film for the script and the performances.
